To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we found a substantial proportion of PLHA who delay, decline, and discontinue ART when it is medically recommended, and this study demonstrates the feasibility to engage these PLHA through peer-referral and hospital clinics.

we recruited a sample of 185 African-American and Latino PLHA who are not taking ART (PLHA-NAT) through HIV hospital clinics (n = 90) and peer-referral (n = 95) and found that recruitment through peer-referral is more feasible than in hospital clinics; that the cohorts were different in age, HIV care engagement, and prior ART use; that levels of ART knowledge were high in both groups; that there were no differences on attitudes toward ART;
we recruited a large sample of African-American and Latino PLHA-NOART, and that we were able to compare clinic- and peer-recruited cohorts on multi-level predictors of ART.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding and addressing barriers to ART among HIV-infected African-Americans and Latino/Hispanics, who are not taking ART.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the findings of this study suggest that the recruitment of HIV-infected individuals who are not on antiretrovial therapy through HIV hospital clinics or through peer-referral was feasible, and that there were some differences between these two groups of individuals.
this study demonstrates the feasibility for engaging PLHA-NOAT through peer-referral, and that peer-recruited PLWA have particularly high rates of barriers to ART.

the study demonstrates the feasibility and utility of using peer-referral as a recruitment strategy to reach HIV-infected individuals who are not on antiretrovival therapy, a vulnerable population that may be difficult to locate through clinic recruitment alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that peer-recruited participants had a higher prevalence of risk factors than those in the clinic.
we found that peer-referral is feasible and may yield a sample of individuals who are less engaged in care than those recruited through clinics.

peer-recruited participants, compared to clinic-recruited, were more likely to be African-American, older, have been living with HIV longer, and have taken ART previously; and they had lower levels of ART engagement, higher rates of ART discontinuation, and higher ART mistrust, and they reported less positive attitudes toward ART.
The main takeaway from our work is that
peer-referral is an effective and efficient method for engaging PLHA-NOART, who are often difficult to reach through clinics.
PLHA-NOAT are a diverse group with varying needs.
PLHA who delay, decline, and discontinue ART are a diverse population, who are not easily recruited in clinics, and that peer referral may be a viable strategy for engaging this population.
